Developing model and redefining reference levels

set.seed(1234)

#including variables that would identify patient risk factors
bone_model = bone %>% 
  select(
    fracture,
    priorfrac,
    age,
    weight,
    height,
    bmi,
    premeno,
    momfrac,
    armassist,
    smoke,
    raterisk,
    fracscore,
    bonemed
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    fracture = relevel(factor(fracture), ref = "No"), #ensures that "No" is the reference outcome
    across(
      c(
        priorfrac, premeno, momfrac, armassist, smoke, bonemed
      ),
      ~ relevel(factor(.x), ref = "No")
    ),
    raterisk = factor( #reference category for preceieved fracture risk
      raterisk,
      levels = c("Less", "Same", "Greater")
    )
  )

glimpse(bone_model)

Train validation split

library(rsample)
set.seed(1234)


bone_split = initial_split(
  bone_model,
  prop = 0.75,
  strata = fracture
)


bone_train = training(bone_split)
bone_test = testing(bone_split)

dim(bone_train)
## [1] 374  13
dim(bone_test)
## [1] 126  13
bind_rows(
  bone_train %>%  mutate(dataset = "Training"),
  bone_test %>%  mutate(dataset = "Validation")
) %>% 
  count(dataset, fracture) %>% 
  group_by(dataset) %>% 
  mutate(
    proportion = n / sum(n),
    percent = scales::percent(proportion, accuracy = 0.1)
  ) %>% 
  ungroup()
#checking for imbalance
bind_rows(
  bone_train %>% 
    summarise(
      dataset = "Training",
      n = n(),
      fracture_rate = mean(fracture == "Yes"),
      mean_age = mean(age),
      mean_bmi = mean(bmi),
      mean_fracscore = mean(fracscore)
    ),
  bone_test %>% 
    summarise(
      dataset = "Validation",
      n = n(),
      fracture_rate = mean(fracture == "Yes"),
      mean_age = mean(age),
      mean_bmi = mean(bmi),
      mean_fracscore = mean(fracscore)
    )
)

summary of training data

library(tidyverse)

#continuous variable
continuous_summary = bone_train %>% 
  group_by(fracture) %>% 
  summarise(
    across(
      c(age, weight, height, bmi, fracscore),
      list(
        mean = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        sd = ~ sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        median = ~ median(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        q1 = ~ quantile(.x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
        q3 = ~ quantile(.x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
      ),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

continuous_summary
#categorical variable
categorical_summary = bone_train %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      priorfrac,
      premeno,
      momfrac,
      armassist,
      smoke,
      raterisk,
      bonemed
    ),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "category"
  ) |>
  count(variable, category, fracture) |>
  group_by(variable, fracture) |>
  mutate(
    percent = 100 * n / sum(n),
    `n (%)` = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", n, percent)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    variable,
    category,
    fracture,
    `n (%)`
  )

plot the training outcome prevalence

bone_train %>% 
  count(fracture) %>% 
  mutate(
    proportion = n / sum(n)
  ) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = fracture, y = proportion)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = scales::percent(
        proportion,
        accuracy = 0.1
      )
    ),
    vjust = -0.4
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent,
    limits = c(0, 0.85)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "First-year fracture prevalence",
    subtitle = "Training data",
    x = "Fracture during first year",
    y = "Percentage of women"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

One-quarter of the women experience a fracture during the 1st year. Because fractures are less common than non-fractures, sensitivity may eventually be more informative than overall accuracy when evaluating prediction models.

continuous predictor

continuous_variable = c(
  "age",
  "weight",
  "height",
  "bmi",
  "fracscore"
)

bone_train %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(continuous_variable),
    names_to = "predictor",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = fracture)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(
    vars(predictor),
    scales = "free",
    ncol = 2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Continuous predictor distributions by fracture status",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Fracture"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

Age: The fracture group is shifted toward older ages. Women who fractured appear more concentrated in the upper-age range, while women without fractures are more concentrated around the early-to-mid 60s. Fracture score: The fracture group is shifted toward higher scores. This suggests fracscore may be an important predictor of first-year fracture. BMI: The two curves overlap heavily, so BMI alone does not appear to strongly separate the fracture groups. Height: There is substantial overlap. Women with fractures may be slightly shorter on average, but the difference looks modest. Weight: The curves are also very similar, with little evidence of strong separation.

The density plots suggest that women who experienced a fracture tended to be older and have higher composite fracture-risk scores. BMI, height, and weight showed substantial overlap between fracture groups, indicating weaker unadjusted relationships with fracture status.

boxplot of continous predcitors by status of fracture

bone_train |>
  select(height, weight, bmi) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  mutate(
    q1 = quantile(value, 0.25),
    q3 = quantile(value, 0.75),
    iqr = IQR(value),
    lower = q1 - 1.5 * iqr,
    upper = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
  ) |>
  filter(value < lower | value > upper) |>
  select(variable, value, lower, upper)
bone_train |>
  mutate(row_id = row_number()) |>
  filter(
    bmi > 40 |
      weight > 110 |
      height < 145 |
      height > 180
  ) |>
  select(row_id, fracture, age, height, weight, bmi)

Age: The fracture group has a higher median age than the no-fracture group. This supports age as a potentially important predictor. Fracture score: The fracture group has a clearly higher median fracscore, with the entire distribution shifted upward. This appears to be the strongest continuous predictor visually. BMI: The medians and interquartile ranges are very similar. There are several high-BMI outliers, especially in the no-fracture group. Height: The fracture group appears slightly shorter on average, but the distributions overlap considerably. Weight: The two groups are very similar, with several high-weight outliers in both groups.

The boxplots show that women who fractured were generally older and had higher composite fracture-risk scores. BMI, height, and weight showed substantial overlap between outcome groups, suggesting weaker unadjusted associations with fracture status.

      y = fracture_rate
    )
  ) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = scales::percent(
        fracture_rate,
        accuracy = 1
      )
    ),
    vjust = -0.3,
    size = 3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    vars(predictor),
    scales = "free_x"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent,
    limits = c(0, NA)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Observed fracture rate by categorical predictor",
    x = NULL,
    y = "First-year fracture rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 30,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )

The categorical EDA suggests that prior fracture, use of arms to stand, maternal fracture history, self-rated fracture risk, and bone medication at enrollment are associated with higher observed fracture rates. Smoking and premenopausal fracture history show little separation between groups.

CAUTION: these are unadjusted rates. For example, the higher fracture rate among women taking bone medication does not mean the medication causes fractures. It may indicate confounding by indication, where women at greater baseline risk are more likely to be prescribed treatment.

FROM EDA Strongest candidate predictors: age bmi fracscore –> composite risk score and can reflect information from variables - like age so use it to compare: individual risk factor model and fracture score model 3 priorfrac armassist momfrac raterisk bonemed

additive logistic regression model

#individual risk factor model where bmi is continuous
model_full_original = glm(
  fracture~ age + bmi + height + weight + priorfrac + momfrac + armassist + smoke + premeno + raterisk + bonemed,
  data = bone_train, family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

#checking for collinearity between height and weight 
bone_train %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = height, y = weight)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship between height and weight",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Pearson correlation =",
      round(cor(bone_train$height, bone_train$weight), 2)
    ),
    x = "Height (cm)",
    y = "Weight (kg)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

#VIF 
# library(car)
# vif_values = vif(model_height_weight)
# vif_values

Height and weight had a modest Pearson correlation of 0.32. Adjusted generalized variance inflation factors were close to 1 for all predictors, indicating no problematic multicollinearity. Therefore, height and weight were retained together.

In logistic regression, GVIF-adjusted values above 2–5 typically indicate meaningful multicollinearity. Values above 10 are considered severe. Here, both BMI and weight exceed 13, and height exceeds 4.5, clearly signaling problematic collinearity.

#question with bmi- to include in additive model or not?
#make bmi categorical
bone_train = bone_train %>% 
  mutate(
    bmi_categorical = cut(
      bmi,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 18.5, 25, 30, Inf),
      labels = c(
        "Underweight",
        "Normal",
        "Overweight",
        "Obesity"
      ),
      right = FALSE
    ),
    bmi_categorical = relevel(bmi_categorical, ref = "Normal")
  )

#individual risk factor model where bmi is continuous
model_cont_bmi = glm(
  fracture~ age + bmi + priorfrac + momfrac + armassist + smoke + premeno + raterisk + bonemed,
  data = bone_train, family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

#bmi categorical model

  model_cont_bmi,
  model_cat_bmi
)
#Comparing using AIC the Cat_BMI with Height+Weight, Height, and Weight
AIC(
  model_cat_bmi,
  model_cat_bmi_height_weight,
  model_cat_bmi_weight,
  model_cat_bmi_height
)
#Comparing Winning Model from above ^ with no BMI with Height+Weight, Height, and Weight
AIC(
  model_cat_bmi_height,
  model_height_weight,
  model_height_only,
  model_weight_only
)

Comparison 1 (Continuous BMI vs Categorical BMI): Our EDA showed that BMI’s relationship with fracture risk was weakly linear, and categorizing BMI removes the linearity assumption while aligning with clinically meaningful thresholds (underweight, normal, overweight, obesity). These categories are widely used in fracture‑risk guidelines and improve interpretability of odds ratios. Because Objective 1 emphasizes interpretability rather than predictive optimization, the categorical BMI model is preferable even if its AIC is marginally higher.

Comparison 2 (Categorical BMI vs Including Height+Weight, Weight, and Height): With additional nuance from other important variables such as height and weight which are basic measures that are easily taken from patient before any examination, which are heavily used as risk factors we may choose to include these additional nuances now that they are not linearly related with another predictor being the BMI which is now categorical. Model with Categorical BMI and Height included had the lower AIC to be the best interetable model and best performing model.

Comparison 3: (Categorical BMI with Height vs No Categorical BMI with Height+Weight, Weight, and Height): Because of our initial analysis its obvious when removing the categorical variable we decrease the complexity which is why AIC’s are lower then the model including the extra categorical BMI predictor with the exeption of the model with weight only (interesting). But since our goals with of interpret-ability are more important for objective 1 we will include keep the categorical predictor for the BMI and include height as it gives the best balance or performance and interpret ability from a clinical perspective.

  fracture ~ age + height + priorfrac + momfrac + armassist + smoke + raterisk + bonemed,
  data = bone_train,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

diagnostic info: model has some observations worth investigating, but there is no evidence of an extreme influence problem.

cook’s d: Several observations were flagged as potentially influential using the 4/n screening rule, but none had an exceptionally large Cook’s distance. These observations were retained and examined through sensitivity analysis.

The increasing concentration of larger bars near the end of the graph is likely because the training rows are ordered or grouped by fracture status. It does not necessarily imply that later observations are inherently problematic.

standarized residuals: Nine observations have standardized residuals above 2, and all nine experienced fractures.Their negative .fitted values are log odds, not probabilities.

need to check whether age, height, and weight (continuous variables) have an about linear relationship with the log odds of fracture

check_logit_linearity = function(data, variable, groups = 5) {
  data %>% 
    mutate(group = ntile(.data[[variable]], groups)) %>% 
    group_by(group) %>% 
    summarise(
      predictor_mean = mean(.data[[variable]], na.rm = TRUE),
      fracture_rate = mean(fracture == "Yes"),
      n = n(),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>% 
    mutate(
      empirical_logit = log(
        (fracture_rate + 0.005) /
          (1 - fracture_rate + 0.005)
      )
    ) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = predictor_mean, y = empirical_logit)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Linearity in the logit:", variable),
      x = variable,
      y = "Empirical log odds of fracture"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}


check_logit_linearity(bone_train, "height")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Height: The empirical log odds generally decrease as height increases. There is some scatter, especially in the shorter groups, but no obvious strong curve. A linear height term is reasonable. Weight: This is the weakest pattern. The middle groups fluctuate, but there is still an overall downward trend. The plot does not show a clear U-shape or other strong systematic curvature, so a linear term is acceptable for the simple additive model.

An empirical-logit plot groups the continuous predictor into bins, calculates the observed fracture proportion in each bin, and transforms that proportion to log odds:

Empirical-logit plots were examined for age, height, and weight. Age showed an approximately linear positive relationship with the log odds of fracture, while height and weight showed generally negative trends with some sampling variability. No strong systematic curvature was observed, so the predictors were retained as linear terms in the additive logistic regression model.

models needed: 1. complex logisitc model 2. LDA 3. QDA 4. Non parametric model

comparison on validation set using –> sensitivity, specificity, prevalence, PPV, NPV, and AUROC Sensitivity asks: “Of the women who fractured, how many did we catch?” Specificity asks: “Of the women who did not fracture, how many did we correctly leave as low risk?” Prevalence asks: “How common was fracture in this sample?”

baseline_metrics

It correctly identifies most women who will not fracture, but it misses many women who actually do fracture.

A sensitivity of 0.219 means the model only identifies about 21.9% of the true fracture cases at the 0.50 threshold.

Because fracture detection is probably the more important goal here, this is a strong reason to revisit the threshold later. A lower threshold should increase sensitivity, though specificity will decrease.

complex logistic regression model

complex_model = glm(
    fracture ~
    age +
    I(age^2) +  #allows fracture risk to accelerate at older ages 
    height +
    priorfrac +
    momfrac +
    armassist +
    smoke +
    raterisk +
    bonemed +
    age:priorfrac + #test whether the effect of prior fracture differs with age
    priorfrac:raterisk, #test whether perceived risk carries different information among woman with vs without a previous fracture
  data = bone_train,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

  complex_model,
  test = "Chisq"
)

We tested a more complex logistic regression model containing a quadratic age term and interactions between age and prior fracture, and between prior fracture and self-rated risk. The complex model had a higher AIC than the additive model (399.93 vs. 395.98), and the likelihood-ratio test was not significant (p=0.399).

Therefore, the added complexity was not supported by the training data, but the model was retained for predictive comparison as required

generate validation predictions for complex logistic model

complex_prediction = bone_test %>% 
  mutate(
    .pred_Yes = predict(
      complex_model,
      newdata = bone_test,
      type = "response"
    ),
    .pred_class = factor(
      if_else(.pred_Yes >= 0.50, "Yes", "No"),
      levels = c("No", "Yes")
    )
  )

# calculate the validation metrics
complex_metrics = tibble(
  Model = "Complex Logistic",
  Threshold = 0.50,

  Sensitivity = yardstick::sens_vec(
    complex_prediction$fracture,
    complex_prediction$.pred_class,
    event_level = "second"
  ),

  Specificity = yardstick::spec_vec(
    complex_prediction$fracture,
    complex_prediction$.pred_class,
    event_level = "second"
  ),

  PPV = yardstick::ppv_vec(
    complex_prediction$fracture,
    complex_prediction$.pred_class,
    event_level = "second"
  ),

  NPV = yardstick::npv_vec(
    complex_prediction$fracture,
    complex_prediction$.pred_class,
    event_level = "second"
  ),

  Prevalence = mean(
    complex_prediction$fracture == "Yes"
  ),

  AUROC = yardstick::roc_auc_vec(
    complex_prediction$fracture,
    complex_prediction$.pred_Yes,
    event_level = "second"
  )
)

complex_metrics

comparing the 2 logistic models

bind_rows(
  baseline_metrics,
  complex_metrics
)

So the complex model gained a little specificity and PPV, but it lost sensitivity and AUROC. Since your main concern is likely identifying women who will fracture, that trade off is not especially attractive. Also, the training AIC and likelihood-ratio test already favored the simpler additive mode

The complex logistic model did not improve predictive discrimination over the additive model. At a 0.50 threshold, it produced slightly higher specificity and PPV, but lower sensitivity and AUROC. Thus, the added interactions and quadratic age term did not appear beneficial.

Normal BMI: fracture probability increases noticeably with age. Obesity: also shows an increasing fracture probability with age, with a somewhat higher estimated risk than normal BMI through much of the age range. Overweight: the curve is nearly flat around 25%, suggesting little age effect within that group. Underweight: the curve decreases sharply with age, but I would be very cautious interpreting this. It likely reflects a small number of underweight observations, especially at older ages.

So visually, the age effect does appear to differ across BMI categories. That gives you some justification to test an interaction:

The age–fracture relationship appeared to differ somewhat across BMI categories, particularly among normal-weight, overweight, and obese women. However, the underweight group contained only seven observations, making its fitted curve highly unstable. Therefore, any apparent interaction involving the underweight category was interpreted cautiously

combining underwegiht & normal for the interaction model

bone_train = bone_train %>%
  mutate(
    bmi_cat2 = case_when(
      bmi < 25 ~ "Under/Normal",
      bmi < 30 ~ "Overweight",
      TRUE ~ "Obesity"
    ),
    bmi_cat2 = factor(
      bmi_cat2,
      levels = c("Under/Normal", "Overweight", "Obesity")
    )
  )

#test
bone_test = bone_test %>%
  mutate(
    bmi_cat2 = case_when(
      bmi < 25 ~ "Under/Normal",
      bmi < 30 ~ "Overweight",
      TRUE ~ "Obesity"
    ),
    bmi_cat2 = factor(
      bmi_cat2,
      levels = c(
        "Under/Normal",
        "Overweight",
        "Obesity"
      )
    )
  )

#new interaction model
complex_bmi_3 = glm(
  fracture ~
    age * bmi_cat2 +
    priorfrac +
    momfrac +
    armassist +
    smoke +
    premeno +
    raterisk +
    bonemed,
  data = bone_train,
  family = binomial
)

FROM THIS: use complex_bmi_interaction3 –> it has essentially the same AIC; it uses fewer parameters, 14 vs. 16; it avoids trying to estimate separate interaction effects using only 7 underweight women; it should therefore be more stable and easier to defend.

We initially modeled BMI using four standard categories and included an age-by-BMI interaction. Because only seven women were underweight, this category produced unstable estimates. We therefore combined underweight and normal BMI. The reduced three-category interaction model had nearly identical AIC to the four-category model (398.71 versus 398.54) while using fewer parameters, so the more parsimonious specification was preferred

So far, none of the models is clearly dominating. The additive logistic model still has the best AUROC by a small amount.

LDA produced discrimination similar to the logistic models, with an AUROC of 0.721. At a 0.50 threshold, its sensitivity remained low at 21.9%, while specificity was high at 91.5%

QDA is catching more true fracture cases, but at the cost of more false positives

QDA improved sensitivity compared with the logistic and LDA models, identifying about 34% of fracture cases at the 0.50 threshold. However, this came with lower specificity and a slightly lower AUROC. This illustrates the tradeoff between sensitivity and specificity and suggests that threshold selection will be important

Your random forest’s largest predicted fracture probability is only 0.496, so at a threshold of 0.50 it literally cannot classify anyone as “Yes” thats why PPV = NaN

At the default 0.50 threshold, the random forest classified all validation observations as non-fractures, yielding 0% sensitivity and 100% specificity. However, its AUROC was 0.699, indicating that the model still had some ability to rank fracture risk. This suggests that 0.50 was an inappropriate threshold for this model.

inspect lower thresholds

#creating function for any prediction df
threshold_metrics = function(data, threshold) {
  
  pred_class = factor(
    if_else(data$.pred_Yes >= threshold, "Yes", "No"),
    levels = c("No", "Yes")
  )
  
  tibble(
    Threshold = threshold,
    Sensitivity = yardstick::sens_vec(
      data$fracture,
      pred_class,
      event_level = "second"
    ),
    Specificity = yardstick::spec_vec(
      data$fracture,
      pred_class,
      event_level = "second"
    ),
    PPV = yardstick::ppv_vec(
      data$fracture,
      pred_class,
      event_level = "second"
    ),
    NPV = yardstick::npv_vec(
      data$fracture,
      pred_class,
      event_level = "second"
    )
  )
}

threshold_grid = seq(0.10, 0.50, by = 0.05)
#threshold_grid = seq(0.10, 0.50, by = 0.01)

rf_thresholds = purrr::map_dfr(
  threshold_grid,
  ~ threshold_metrics(rf_prediction, .x)
)

rf_thresholds

The default 0.50 threshold was inappropriate for the random forest because all predicted fracture probabilities were below 0.50. Lower thresholds were evaluated, and a threshold around 0.24–0.25 provided a more balanced sensitivity-specificity tradeoff.

One important methodological point: ideally, the exact threshold should be chosen using the training/CV data, not optimized directly on the validation set. Since you already used the validation set to inspect thresholds, I would avoid claiming that 0.25 is an independently validated optimal threshold. F

additive_final_metrics = tibble(
  Model = "Additive Logistic",
  Threshold = 0.21,
  Sensitivity = yardstick::sens_vec(
    additive_final$fracture,
    additive_final$.pred_class,

    additive_final$fracture,
    additive_final$.pred_class,

combining all the models final metrics

final_model_comparison = bind_rows(
  additive_final_metrics,
  complex_final_metrics,
  complex_cat_bmi_final_metrics,
  complex_cat_bmi_final_metrics3,
  lda_final_metrics,
  qda_final_metrics,
  rf_final_metrics
)

final_model_comparison

Additive Logistic still has the highest AUROC: 0.723 LDA is very close: 0.721 Original Complex Logistic: 0.718 First categorical-BMI complex model: about 0.718 Second categorical-BMI complex model: 0.666, which is clearly worse Random Forest: 0.699

Adding categorical BMI and age-by-BMI interaction terms did not improve out-of-sample predictive performance. One categorical-BMI model performed similarly to the original complex logistic model, while the more heavily modified version performed substantially worse. This suggests the added BMI complexity was not helpful for prediction.

And for LDA/QDA:

LDA performed nearly identically to logistic regression, while QDA offered no meaningful improvement. This suggests that allowing class-specific covariance structures did not substantially improve discrimination.

Just keep complex model without cat bmi or different bucket of bmi in the final ROC curve comparision

ROC curve comparision

roc_data = bind_rows(
  yardstick::roc_curve(
    baseline_prediction,
    truth = fracture,
    .pred_Yes,
    event_level = "second"
  ) %>% 
    mutate(Model = "Additive Logistic"),

  yardstick::roc_curve(
    complex_prediction,
    truth = fracture,
    .pred_Yes,
    event_level = "second"
  ) %>% 
    mutate(Model = "Complex Logistic"),
  
  
  yardstick::roc_curve(
    lda_prediction,
    truth = fracture,
    .pred_Yes,
    event_level = "second"
  ) %>% 
    mutate(Model = "LDA"),

  yardstick::roc_curve(
    qda_prediction,
    truth = fracture,
    .pred_Yes,
    event_level = "second"
  ) %>% 
    mutate(Model = "QDA"),

  yardstick::roc_curve(
    rf_prediction,
    truth = fracture,
    .pred_Yes,
    event_level = "second"
  ) %>% 
    mutate(Model = "Random Forest")
)

#plotting it
roc_data %>% 
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = 1 - specificity,
      y = sensitivity,
      color = Model
    )
  ) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = 2
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "ROC Curves for Validation Data",
    x = "1 - Specificity",
    y = "Sensitivity",
    color = "Model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

All five curves are above the diagonal reference line, so all models discriminate better than random guessing. The curves are very close together, which matches the AUROCs clustered around 0.70–0.72. The additive logistic model has the highest AUROC, but only by a small margin. Random Forest does not show a clear improvement despite being more flexible.

#discussion of LDA/QDA assumptions LDA and QDA assumptions were only approximately satisfied. Several predictors were categorical, and the continuous predictors did not appear perfectly multivariate normal within fracture groups. LDA additionally assumes equal covariance matrices across groups, while QDA relaxes that requirement. Because predictive performance was similar to logistic regression, these assumption violations did not appear to produce a major practical advantage for either discriminant-analysis model
